keyPhrases.de: Können Sie mir fünf Euro wechseln?
keyPhrases.text: Can you change five euros for me?
Excuse me, where can I find flour?

keyPhrases.de: Ich hätte gern 200 Gramm Gouda, bitte.
keyPhrases.text: I'd like 200 grams of Gouda, please.
I have a bag with me.

subtitles.text: I'm so hungry! But my fridge is empty.
Then off to the supermarket!
Supermarket? All in German?
Of course! Today you do a whole shopping trip – from the shopping cart to the receipt.
And in every situation we ask you: What do you say?
And you only have five seconds!
You want a shopping cart. But you need a coin for it – and you only have a five-euro note.
An older man is standing next to you.
What do you say?
A: Excuse me, can you give me five euros as a present?
B: Excuse me, can you change five euros for me?
C: Excuse me, I want your cart.
B! „Wechseln“ means: you give a note and get coins back. „Schenken“
means: you get it for free – that would be very nice, but a bit cheeky.
One moment … yes: two, four, five euros. Here you go!
Thank you very much!
Repeat after me!
Can you change five euros for me?
You need flour. But where is the flour? An employee is stocking a shelf.
What do you ask?
A: Excuse me, where can I find flour?
B: „Wo ist der Mehl?“ (wrong article)
C: Have you found flour?
B! „Wo ist der Mehl?“
Almost, Leo. It's „das Mehl“. But A is even better: „Entschuldigung, wo finde ich …?“
(Excuse me, where can I find …?) – that's how you politely ask for anything in the supermarket.
Flour is in aisle three, right at the bottom of the shelf.
Thank you!
Repeat after me!
Excuse me, where can I find flour?
Aisle three, right at the bottom.
Now you go to the fresh food counter. You want some Gouda.
Hello! What can I get you?
What do you say?
A: I am 200 grams of Gouda.
B: Yes, it may be.
C: I'd like 200 grams of Gouda, please.
C! „Was darf's sein?“ simply means: What would you like? And with „Ich hätte gern …“
(I'd like …) you always order politely – at the counter, at the bakery, in a café.
Repeat after me!
I'd like 200 grams of Gouda, please.
Frau Haas cuts the cheese. The scale shows: 230 grams.
Is a little more okay?
What do you say?
A: No, I'm not allowed.
B: Yes, that's fine.
C: Yes, I am a little more.
B! You hear this sentence at every counter in Germany. It means: it's a bit more than you ordered – is that okay?
If not, just say: „Nein, bitte genau 200 Gramm.“ (No, exactly 200 grams, please.)
Anything else?
No, thanks. That's all.
Repeat after me!
Yes, that's fine.
No, thanks. That's all.
You keep walking. Suddenly you hear an announcement. Listen carefully!
Dear customers! On offer today: bananas, only 99 cents per kilo.
How much is a kilo of bananas?
C: 99 cents
C! 99 cents. „Im Angebot“ means: cheaper today than usual.
Repeat after me!
The bananas are on offer.
You also have empty bottles with you – with this symbol: deposit („Pfand“). Where do they go?
A: To the deposit machine. You get money back.
B: Into the bin at the entrance.
C: To the checkout – as a present.
B, into the trash!
No, Leo – then you're throwing money away! A! For many bottles you get 25 cents back.
The machine gives you a voucher. You hand it in at the checkout.
Repeat after me!
Where is the deposit machine?
Now you're at the checkout. You put everything on the belt.
Hello! Do you collect points?
What do you say?
A: Yes, I collect stamps.
B: I collect your points.
C: No, thanks.
A! I collect stamps. Since school.
Nice, Leo – but she doesn't want to know that. C! Many supermarkets have a card or app with points.
If you don't have one, just say: „Nein, danke.“
Repeat after me!
No, thanks.
Yes, here is my card.
Do you need a bag?
What do you say?
A: Yes, a bag of milk, please.
B: No, thanks. I have a bag with me.
C: No, I am not a bag.
B! Good to know: bags almost always cost money in Germany.
Many people bring their own bag.
Repeat after me!
I have a bag with me.
That's €23.47. Are you paying cash or by card?
What do you say?
A: By card, please.
B: I pay with „Bar“.
C: Yes, cash or card.
C! Yes!
Leo … that's not a yes-or-no question! A! „Bar“ means: with notes and coins. And if you're not sure, ask: „Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?“
(Can I pay by card?)
Repeat after me!
By card, please.
Can I pay by card?
Would you like the receipt?
What do you say?
A: No, I don't like candy („Bonbons“).
B: No, thanks. I don't need it.
C: Yes, I'd like the checkout.
A! I don't like candy. Too much sugar.
Leo! A „Bon“ is not a „Bonbon“. The „Kassenbon“ is the slip of paper – it shows what you bought.
B is correct. Or: „Ja, bitte.“ (Yes, please.)
Have a nice day!
Thanks, you too!
Repeat after me!
Thanks, you too!
Three tips for the supermarket in Germany.
First: on Sunday almost all supermarkets are closed – so shop on Saturday!
Second: at the checkout you put everything on the belt yourself.
The divider bar shows: the next customer starts here.
And third: things move fast at the checkout.
Pack your things calmly after the checkout – that's completely normal.
Leo is writing a shopping list. But something's not right …
A bottle of yogurt.
A cup of yogurt!
A can of bread.
A loaf of bread – or a pack of toast!
A cup of pasta.
A pack of pasta!
A pack of water.
A bottle of water!
A bag of tomatoes.
A can of tomatoes!
„Wo finde ich der Käse?“
„Den Käse“! „Wo finde ich den Käse?“ (Where can I find the cheese?)
And the verb goes to the end: not „Ich möchte bezahlen mit Karte“, but: „Ich möchte mit Karte bezahlen.“ (I'd like to pay by card.)
And at the checkout: the „Bon“ is the receipt. A „Bonbon“ is a sweet.
And now everything once more. The ten most important sentences. Repeat after me!
Can you change five euros for me?
Excuse me, where can I find flour?
I'd like 200 grams of Gouda, please.
Yes, that's fine.
No, thanks. That's all.
The bananas are on offer.
Where is the deposit machine?
I have a bag with me.
Can I pay by card?
Thanks, you too!
What do you like to buy most at the supermarket? Write it in the comments!
Bye, and see you soon at LilyLingua!
